(a) durational cues are integrated in a continuous fashion during the process of word identification and that (b) acoustic-phonetic cues to lexical choice are asymmetrically weighted in the lexical interpretation process.

In summary, our research is concerned with
how acoustic-phonetic cues are used in the process of lexical choice and how these cues are mapped onto the phonemic level.
the manner in which the phonetic information in the speech signal is mapped onto lexical representations.
the way in which acoustic information is used by the speech processor in mapping onto the lexicon.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lexical system is a complex structure that is sensitive to a wide variety of acoustic cues.

the acoustic-phonetic input to the word recognition process is a complex function of the acoustic signal, the lexical structure of the language, the phonological structure of the lexicon, and the phonetic structure of the lexemes.

acoustic cues are mapped onto the lexical representation in a way that is consistent with a model in which the phonological representation is accessed before the lexical level, and that the lexical representation is accessed before lexical selection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

lexical access and selection are not necessarily sequential processes, and that the lexical interpretation of phonetic cues is a dynamic process in which acoustic cues are integrated over time and across different dimensions of the signal.
lexical access is not a process of matching a single acoustic pattern to a lexical representation but rather a process of matching acoustic patterns to multiple representations in parallel.

the mapping of acoustic cues onto phonological structure is an interactive process, in which the acoustic information is interpreted and the lexical interpretation in turn influences the interpretation of the acoustic information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mapping between acoustic-phonetic and lexical representations is not arbitrary and that phonetic information is not processed independently of the lexicon.
the acoustic-phonetic properties of a word are mapped onto the lexical system through the use of partial cues.

phonological knowledge can be used to constrain lexical access, and the results of the second experiment suggest that the mapping between phonetic information and phonological knowledge is not necessarily symmetric.
